utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the hearing of motions by the accused in relation to provisional release. These, in effect, are second applications by these accused, on the basis that there is new material which should be considered. We will hear briefly submissions on both sides. I think we've got to have the case called first, though. Perhaps we had better start with that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-99-37-PT, the Prosecutor versus Milan Milutinovic, Nikola Sainovic, and Dragoljub Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And the appearances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appear today with Cristina Romano, Mr. Milbert Shin and case manager Susan Grogan. Geoffrey Nice is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We didn't get any translation I'm afraid of that. Can you have another go, Mr. Fila and we see if we do a bit better.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, once again, my name is Toma Fila and I represent Mr. Sainovic, together with Mr. Petrovic, an attorney at law from Belgrade. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Tomislav Visnjic and Peter Robinson, for Defence of Mr. Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. As I was saying, this is an application for provisional release by these accused. We have read the various pleadings, so there's no need to repeat them. One further thing is this: That a representative of the embassy, Mr. Panceski, is in Court. Perhaps you would care to introduce yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANCESKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Miodrag Panceski. I am first secretary of the embassy of Serbia and Montenegro here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There has been an application by the Prosecution to cross-examine the representative of the government. We've considered that. We will allow the representative, Mr. Panceski, to make a statement. We will not allow cross-examination. We consider it inappropriate for a representative of the government to be cross-examined in these circumstances. But we will hear submissions. Mr. Fila, for you to begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is for the second time that the Defence has submitted a request for provisional release of Mr. Sainovic. According to the Rules of this Tribunal, I have the right to do that only if I present new arguments, arguments that I did not present the first time. In order to avoid repetition, because I have expressed my arguments in my motion, and further in the reply to the response of the Prosecutor, I shall just briefly state and summarise these arguments. In the meantime, Mr. Sainovic arrived in the Detention Unit in Scheveningen -- excuse me, Mr. Milutinovic arrived in the Detention Unit in Scheveningen. Therefore, all of the accused are now here present at the Tribunal, which is yet another proof that the guarantees offered by Serbia and Montenegro have been fulfilled. If I may remind Their Honours, Mr. Sarkic stated that he would be brought here, he would come here after the expiration of the mandate of Mr. Sainovic. Therefore, the argument of the Prosecutor that Mr. Milutinovic is not yet here is no longer valid. The second matter that needs to be addressed at this point is the fact that a union of Serbia and Montenegro has been created in the meantime. It has been duly constituted. It has its president and its ministers, and I am very pleased to be able to state before this Tribunal that the first president of this union stated in his first address after he had become the president that the cooperation with the Tribunal would be much better than in the past, because he's a representative of the group of people who had always advocated cooperation with the Tribunal. This has also been stated by the president of the Assembly of Serbia and Montenegro. This was further exposed and expressed in a letter addressed to the Council of Europe, as a promise that this cooperation with continue in the future. This promise has been accepted by the Council of Europe, and it is expected that Serbia and Montenegro will become members of the Council of Europe in the near future. That was the second very important issue that I wanted to draw your attention to. So if the Council of Europe believes that the cooperation with the Tribunal will continue, then I think it is only fair to assume that this Tribunal should also trust this guarantee. In the meantime, Serbia has made significant progress in terms of cooperation with the Tribunal. I have already mentioned the arrival of Mr. Milutinovic, and even Mr. Seselj. There is another fact that supports this view. Many of the documents are no longer considered to be the secret of the state. The Prosecutor, as far as I am aware, is now able to obtain access to all witnesses that they wish to interview. They are involved in a number of discussions and conversations with the local authorities, members of the Ministry of the Interior and the former members of the SBS, and we can therefore conclude that this cooperation will be finalised with the handover of all the documents that are still outstanding. It is also very important to note that Mr. Sainovic enjoyed immunity as a federal deputy at the time and that the state of Serbia never sheltered him from the arrival of The Hague. He was never told that he should wait for his immunity to expire and then to surrender to the Tribunal. Quite the contrary; it was only necessary for the appropriate law on cooperation with this Tribunal to be adopted, and Mr. Sainovic voluntarily appeared before this Tribunal, never having relied upon the immunity that he enjoyed. I wanted to state this because I wanted to remind Their Honours that he will definitely not enjoy any special treatment by the state, for the fact that he used to have immunity before. The current situation in Serbia is an encouragement for us and should be interpreted as an encouragement for the international community as a whole. However, I have to mention the assassination of the Prime Minister, which is a tragic and regrettable incident. However, the new Prime Minister has also expressed as one of his priorities the cooperation -- the ongoing and continuing cooperation with this Tribunal. The state undertook a number of energetic steps and established full control in the Republic of Serbia. The situation has never been as safe as it is now, and it is quite clear that the state of Serbia will be in the position to fulfil its commitments and its obligations should you grant our application. The next thing that I wish to remind you of is the following: Ms. Del Ponte and the OTP before her stated three main requirements that need to be discussed in relation with the provisional release. The first one being voluntary surrender, the second one the guarantees, and the third one interview with the Prosecutor. The Appeals Chamber insisted in particular on the behaviour and the conduct of the accused prior to the arrival in the Tribunal, in order to assess whether and to what extent that surrender was indeed voluntary. The Appeals Chamber held that the key indicator of the voluntary character of the surrender, prior statements made by the accused in relation to the arrival of the accused. I don't know how, but it seems to have been stated in one of the motions that Mr. Sainovic had stated that he would never voluntarily surrender to the Tribunal, that he would never appear before the Tribunal. We, as a Defence, and Mr. Sainovic himself, clearly stated that he had never stated any such statements. There have never been any statements made by Mr. Sainovic in connection with his non-willingness to appear or his lack of respect towards the Tribunal. Furthermore, the Prosecutor forwarded a number of statements that I made before I became Defence counsel of Mr. Sainovic. I don't know Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. whether these statements were correct or not. They were published in a number of articles. But I think that they might become important should the Chamber deliberate rate on the provisional release, that is, what I stated in this regard. I think that it is not relevant what I stated before I became counsel of Mr. Sainovic, that is, before the 24th of April last year. Bearing in mind various experiences with the OTP and others, at the moment of surrender, I insisted that the power of attorney should be first signed by the deputy minister of justice, and you will find the signature of Mr. Sarkic on the document that you have, that is, the date when the power of attorney was received. A copy of the power of attorney can be found at the Court. I proceeded in that manner out of abundance of caution. So whatever I declared prior to the 24th of April, if I had indeed declared anything of that kind, was declared on my own, on a private basis, and it is the nature of our profession. It is true that Mr. Sainovic was waiting for a legal basis to act, and that was the act -- the law on cooperation with the Tribunal. When the law was adopted, he immediately took steps in order to surrender. You will also find a statement which was given in relation to the arrest of Mr. Krajisnik, which the Prosecutor is interpreting as a position of Mr. Sainovic. I explained this in detail in my written statement. I said that it was not important, not relevant. It was merely a press communique of the government. He was not referring to what he intended to do. So to sum up, you do not dispose of any single interview any single statement or declaration. I'm not here discussing the veracity or the correctness of such statements to that effect. So the first basis that is the lack of respect vis-a-vis the Tribunal does not exist. As for the second requirement, that is, the guarantees, I have already stated that the arrival of Mr. Milutinovic is yet another proof that Serbia and Montenegro are fulfilling their obligations, and I also mentioned the fact that there is a strong intention to pursue this cooperation, as we have seen from the first address of the new Prime Minister. The third requirement which was mentioned by Ms. Del Ponte here before the Chamber was the fact that it was very important for the Office of the Prosecutor that the accused should give statement or give interview to the Prosecutor and that should that be complied with, then she indicated her willingness to agree with the request for provisional release. I took it upon myself to ensure that should Mr. Sainovic be in Belgrade, that interview be conducted. The Appeals Chamber reversed your decision in that respect; however, I have not changed my decision in any way, because the objective was not blackmail, that is to say, if you let me go, I will talk, if you don't let me go, I won't talk. We're not children. We understand what this is all about. When the decision of the Appeals Chamber was adopted, Mr. Sainovic indeed started to talk to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Appeals Chamber on that point upheld the Trial Chamber's view that whether the Prosecutor was going to interview an accused or not is irrelevant, as far as provisional release is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. At any rate, I wish to state here before the Chamber that we have fulfilled the obligations that we undertook. I merely wish to indicate for this Chamber that we abide by our commitments. This is also a demonstration of the conduct of the accused before the Chamber, the fact that he's willing to fulfil his commitments, notwithstanding the importance that you will attach to this. Mr. Sainovic has so far conducted nine days of interview with the Prosecutor. It seems that the Prosecutor is not satisfied with this interview. I have never found anywhere in the Rules that the Prosecutor should be satisfied with the interview. If I understand the Prosecutor correctly, they would only be satisfied if the accused confessed to what is alleged against him in the indictment. But in that case, he would not need an interview; it would be enough for him to get up and enter a plea of guilty, and that would be the end of the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is further very important to say that this interview was indeed conducted, and I also wish to say that it was not -- it would not be possible to interfere -- for the accused to interfere with the witnesses in any way, because he has already made his statement, and that can be used against him. So the interview was yet another demonstration of the great respect on the part of the accused for this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, you mentioned that many documents that were formerly secret no longer have that status and that therefore the Prosecutor would be able to have access to them. How did that come about that these documents which were formerly secret no longer have that status?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our media, and I have inquired personally, Mr. Kostunica, before leaving, in consultation with the supreme council of the Defence, removed the seal of secret of state from most of the documents. So what the president of the former Yugoslavia had as a civilian person is now available. I think this is very important. It is important to know this, because this material is available. That is to say, what Mr. Nice is stating in a memo in relation to the command in Pristina no longer is valid. The seal of -- the secret of the state has been removed from most of the documents. I am referring to the minutes from the meetings with Mr. Milosevic throughout the year of 1998, and so on and so forth. They were also given during the interview minutes from the SBS meeting, some of them. The fact remains that the committee for cooperation with this Tribunal is not supplying the Defence with the same kind of documents they're supplying the Prosecutor with. But this is our problem. However, we know that this has happened. The decision of Mr. Kostunica prior to his departure is valid and applicable, and a large number of documents have been sent in the meantime. This is all I can inform you about. And with Their Honours' indulgence, I should like to ask for a private session for just a couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And to conclude, by way of conclusion, let me just appeal to Your Honours to grant this motion and to do so for several reasons, one of them being the cooperation of our state with the Tribunal. That cooperation cannot be a one-way cooperation. With your permission, Your Honour, I have a lot of experience. Once we were "happy" with the influence of the Soviet Union and the former Yugoslavia. They used the word "davaj," "give" whenever they requested anything, whether it was corn or machines, or anything else. They never gave us anything. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. They always wanted us to give them something. Sometimes I think that this cooperation can be compared with that. We are very often asked to give but very rarely are we given anything. I think that some steps from the opposing side, in terms of cooperation, such as provisional releases, or some other act of goodwill, good faith, would indeed help this new government to start working. You can interpret this as an appeal of a lawyer and an experienced person who has lived for a very long time in that country. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and members of the Trial Chamber. I think our starting point for consideration of provisional release at this stage has to be the Appeals Chamber's opinion and the two errors of law which it held occurred in the first proceedings before this Trial Chamber. In response to the Prosecutor's argument concerning the failure to arrest President Milutinovic, it was held that the Trial Chamber erred in failing to explicitly consider the senior position of the accused as it related to the guarantees from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbia. Now, after the Appeals Chamber decision, there has been a change in circumstances. President Milutinovic has arrived in The Hague and there is now not a single former -- person of senior position in the government of either the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or the Republic of Serbia who remains a fugitive. They are all here, Milosevic, Milutinovic, Sainovic, Ojdanic, and even Seselj. It simply cannot now be said that because of his former senior position, General Ojdanic might somehow be shielded from arrest. Lest there be any doubt on this point, we would note the presence of the representative of the government of Serbia and Montenegro, who I believe will affirm that his government stands firmly behind the guarantee for General Ojdanic, that he will be arrested if he violates the conditions of his release, notwithstanding his former senior position, and to reaffirm that after the tragic events of two weeks ago in Serbia, the government of Serbia and Montenegro remains firmly committed to supervise and enforce its guarantees to this Tribunal. I would point out that it was the late Prime Minister Djindjic who personally signed the guarantee of the Republic of Serbia in support of General Ojdanic. The second error of law that was identified by the Appeals Chamber was the failure to explicitly consider the public statements of the accused as they related to whether his surrender to this Tribunal was voluntary. Of course, all you had before you was a footnote in the Prosecutor's brief which referenced a headline to one story, and we now have provided you with all of the public statements of the accused as annex 1 to our application. It is our submission that consideration of the full panoply of General Ojdanic's public statements, demonstrates that his surrender was voluntary. But lest there be any doubt about that, we have provided you with a second personal guarantee, an affidavit of General Ojdanic, in which he details the circumstances which lead to his surrender and explained the public statements reported in the newspapers. It is our request that General Ojdanic be allowed to give evidence today. I would propose that you allow me less than five minutes to have him identify and affirm the contents of his affidavit and that the Prosecutor then be allowed to cross-examine him. In this way you will not be deciding this important motion based upon what one reads in newspapers but upon the tried and true reliable method of sworn testimony tested by cross-examination. And of course, if you prefer, I conduct a full direct examination, I can do so. We submit that you, as a Trial Chamber, got it right the first time when you held that General Ojdanic had established that he would appear for trial and not be a danger to others. And when you exercised your discretion in favour of his provisional release. The circumstances since your original decision have borne that out. We urge you to hear from General Ojdanic and the representative from Serbia and Montenegro today so that you and the Appeals Chamber have a full record upon which to decide this issue of great importance to General Ojdanic, his family, and his Defence. Finally, I would note that we have received information that the Prosecutor is no longer opposing the provisional release for the co-accused Milutinovic, and if this is true it would be relevant to these proceedings, because we are relying on the very same guarantees and therefore I would ask that this matter be addressed by the Prosecutor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we've heard that, but we will hear from the Prosecutor. We'll consider whether to hear some live evidence or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, we are against you about the General giving evidence. We've got his affidavit. We don't think it's appropriate for evidence to be given at this stage. But of course, if you want to add anything to what you've already said upon it, it's open to you to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I don't wish to add anything further. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Panceski, if you would like to address us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANCESKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Your Honours, it is an honour to address you today on behalf of Serbia and Montenegro. On the occasion of the motion by the Defence counsel of Nikola Sainovic, Dragoljub Ojdanic for provisional release, I wish to inform you that the guarantees that the federal government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia gave at its 51st session held on the 17th of May, 2002 are still valid. This means that the government of Serbia and Montenegro continues to guarantee that should the Tribunal grant provisional release of the accused until the start of trial, the competent authorities in Serbia and Montenegro will comply with all orders of this Tribunal and that the accused will appear at any time they are summoned before the International Criminal Tribunal. These guarantees include all the obligations, including escorting the accused while they are travelling, monitoring of their stay in the territory of Serbia and Montenegro, regular reporting to the Tribunal, and their possible -- their arrest should it become necessary, should they not appear when called upon. This is all based on Article 46 of the law on the cooperation of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia with the International Criminal Tribunal. The government of Serbia and Montenegro considers that the accused surrendered voluntarily, and Mr. Sainovic, although one of the leading politicians of Milosevic's regime, after the democratic changes, remained at liberty for a long time in Yugoslavia, after the indictment was issued. He was one of the first to respond to the call by his government to surrender voluntarily. Mr. Ojdanic did the same. They never tried hide, and what is more important, their decision to surrender, although it did depend on the democratic changes in Yugoslavia, was theirs alone. They were not forced to appear before this Tribunal. In view of the fact that the government of Serbia and Montenegro has a legal duty to provide guarantees to all persons who surrender voluntarily, a positive decision by the Trial Chamber in this case would contribute greatly to others deciding to take the same step. Your Honours, the provisional release of Messrs. Ojdanic and Sainovic, with the appropriate measures, would not, in our view, represent a risk for the further successful running of this trial. This follows from the seriousness with which the government of my country approached the execution of all its obligations to cooperate with the Tribunal, the Office of the Prosecutor, and Defence counsel. This process continues. Serbia and Montenegro has so far extradited six persons including the former head of state. A large number of accused have surrendered Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. voluntarily, supported by a campaign instituted by the government of my country. Cooperation with regard to locating witnesses and their release from the obligation to keep state secrets is complete, and under Rule 54 bis in the Milosevic case, cooperation continues. In all cases where this Tribunal has so far accepted the guarantees of my government, and that is Biljana Plavsic, Pavle Strugar, Mr. Jokic, Strugar, and Talic, there have been no difficulties. All these persons are replying to all summons and there have been no objections to the way my government has acted in these cases. That is why we believe that this Chamber and the Office of the Prosecutor and the Defence will treat the guarantees provided by Serbia and Montenegro with all due respect and encourage our further efforts, with a view to cooperation. Your Honours, I wish now to refer to one more point and add to what Mr. Fila said when responding to His Honour Judge Robinson's question relating to the confidentiality of documents. I wish to add to the Defence counsel's response by saying that the seal of confidentiality was removed from these documents by a decision of the Supreme Defence Council, which is the only body authorised in my country to make such decisions. This decision was not made by the former president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Vojislav Kostunica, personally, but it was made by this body. Mr. Kostunica, as the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in his capacity as such, was the chairperson of the Supreme Defence Council. The removal of the seal of confidentiality from a certain number of documents was done on the basis of the law on cooperation with the Tribunal and at the request or upon a certain number of requests received from the Office of the Prosecutor. This is all I have to say at present, Your Honours. I thank you for your attention and for hearing me today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Panceski.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I reply in the order in which addresses have been advanced, I noted that Mr. Robinson had information to the effect we were not opposing provisional release of Mr. Milutinovic. I don't know what he means by that. There is no support for that. As I understand it, from my own dealings and as I am instructed by others involved. It may be before I reply that we'll be assisted by further details of what is meant by information to that effect. But I can't deal with it on that basis other than to explain the position as it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In order, then, and with a few additional points, of course the relevant starting point is the Appeal Chamber decision which found fundamentally that these accused had not surrendered voluntarily. Nothing in the pleadings changes that position. Dealing with the points made by Mr. Fila, so far as the surrender of Mr. Milutinovic is concerned, what is important is that he remained a fugitive, guarded by the state, and in his own interest, as long as it suited him. There is nothing to be gained by the fact that he has eventually surrendered. The suggestion that cooperation is going to be better simply underlines that despite earlier assertions, it has been substantially imperfect in the past, leaving room for improvement, promises of improvement to come, what are always given in courts. It is, of course, delivery that matters. Picking up on a point just made on behalf of the government about compliance with obligations in respect of making witnesses available and continuing compliance under 54 bis, I'm certainly not aware that the authorities have made every conceivable arrangement for every witness. On the contrary; as the Chamber will well know from a recent hearing, there are two extremely important witnesses, not available to us, one not available long term, because of, as the Chamber expressed it, really, understandable, remaining uncertainty about the terms of a waiver. And as to another witness in particular, and this is just two of it may be several or many, in relation to another witness, there was simply no explanation offered of any kind why that witness was only being provided a waiver in respect of one period when his evidence was absolutely valuable and would be absolutely valuable in respect of two other periods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Nice, they would want you to look at the picture more generally and to suggest that there has been an overall improvement resulting from this lifting of the secrecy on certain documents. That's not your experience?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. As I think I said at the earlier hearing, which I think itself was an open hearing, so I break no rules in repeating it, it's one thing to provide a lot of documents that are not particularly significant if the comparatively limited number that you withhold are the absolutely critical ones. That's the point we made then, the point we make now. And the Chamber will recall that we, on this particular topic, made two other points: One, and it has another echo in this particular hearing, that there's the world of difference between a body, a government, that says we'll actually actively go out to help this Tribunal, find the material that will assist it and turn up for us, a hundred, 200 documents that will enable this case to be done and dusted in the vernacular, months ago. Not this case, the other case. That's one thing. That's of course not what happens. These states wait until we prise information or material out of them, and that what they say what they then seek to describe as cooperation. But coming from that general point that I made before, we come to the particular point that featured in the 54 bis application and features in the pleadings here, archives. The absolute basic material within which documents might be found. The Prosecution always seeking not to have generalised access to the archives but the ability to know what archives exist to survey indexes, indices and so on, in order to be able to take their particular requests for resisted to the hilt by the authorities. And yet, and I think Mr. Sainovic's own application, we discover, as we explained in the 54 bis hearing, that archives are apparently available to the accused in some way or another, not known to us. So in answer to Your Honour's question, has there been a significant improvement, of course there's been a change and improvement over time, as the authorities have changed. But the position has been clearly articulated in various international forums by the Prosecutor, and in this forum by me, and there's no reason to, as it were, doubt the good faith of the OTP in its representations about cooperation, because where cooperation exists, then we have every reason to say it exists, both because we have no reason to say otherwise and also because of the knock-on beneficial effects it would have, and we've seen examples of real cooperation and of our response to it. Mr. Shin was good enough to provide a little chart for me to have a look at. And apart from all the details of the Plavsic case, which the Chamber is particularly acquainted, it's important to have in mind as well that very approximately, the man Jokic surrendered one month and one week, or thereabouts, after knowing of his indictment, conditional provisional release I think not opposed. Strugar, 19 days, provisional release not opposed. Martic and Mrksic, on the other hand, over six years each, and understandably, properly, and sustainably on appeal, of course provisional release was opposed. And so the Prosecution has always taken a measured and fair approach, picking up one of the suggestions from the later or latest submissions by those representing the accused or the government, has taken a measured approach and has responded to proper acts of cooperation where they've existed. But, and it's our duty to do this, we've reflected non-cooperation and resistance where it is identified. And so cooperation, it's said, will be better in the future. There may be improvement, there may not. There is a very volatile area, and indeed a dangerous area, as we know, with forces of work that are not just the forces of government, it would appear, forces that may reflect interests other than political or governmental, forces that may reflect, in some of the steps they take, what's going on here. We can't help that. All we know is that we face a regime that has this volatility in its past that may have volatility in the future. The new arrangement between Serbia and Montenegro is itself subject to referenda as soon as I think three years' time, forecasting further change in the structure of that body. So as to cooperation by the state or the state bodies, of no value and not proven and far, far from complete, or even far from good. The Chamber will also have had in mind, or will have in mind, that this protestation of cooperation by those bodies has to be set beside the law that was introduced in April 2002, which required that all people thereafter to be indicted by this Tribunal would not be handed over to this Tribunal because they should be tried in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. We have that law in English, if it's helpful to the Chamber to follow. Mr. Fila, on behalf of Mr. Sainovic, sought to deal with the statements made by him. Can I take you to them, if my learned friend would be good enough just to hand me the relevant part. But while he's doing that, the Chamber will have heard Mr. Fila assert that statements made by him, Mr. Fila, on behalf of somebody identified as his client are in some way not the statements of his client, simply because he hadn't yet become formally the appointed counsel of this Tribunal. That I find a difficult assertion to accept. There is a presumption that a lawyer speaks on behalf of his client, unless rejected, I suppose, and where it happened, as I think it did here, when we find it, twice, that presumption surely becomes irrebuttably strong. It's always the way when we carefully prepare the documents, knowing which ones we're going to refer to. They go and get themselves buried in something else. But I wouldn't worry about it. If you'll just give me a minute, they will turn up. There they are, already marked and tagged by Mr. Shin. They can be found on our response to the second application of Mr. Sainovic for provisional release. The registry number is 7699 at the top right-hand corner and the quoted observations of Mr. Fila are these, said to have been made on the 22nd of March of as recently as the year 2002: Third line down: "`Former Yugoslav deputy Prime Minister Nikola Sainovic will not surrender to the UN war crimes Tribunal in The Hague,' his lawyer said Friday. `I know that he does not want to surrender voluntarily,' said Mr. Fila." The second quotation recorded as coming from Mr. Fila on the following page, with his comments about speculations that the former vice-president will surrender to the Tribunal: "Toma Fila, a lawyer of the former vice-president of the Yugoslav government and of Serbian Socialist Party official Nikola Sainovic, dismissed public speculations about his client's readiness to voluntarily surrender to The Hague Tribunal. "`I know that Sainovic does not want to go voluntarily to The Hague and his party the SPS has the same position, i.e., voluntary surrender would cause him problems with the party and he would have to bear that in mind,' Fila stated." And on the following page, an earlier reference coming from June 2000, under the heading "Topic: International political leader military," two-thirds of the way down the page, and commenting on Mr. Krajisnik's arrest. And it matters not that it was somebody else's arrest rather than his own. It's his attitude to the Tribunal that counts, and counts conclusively against him, in our submission. "Commenting on Momcilo Krajisnik's arrest, Sainovic said that the Yugoslav government had sent a strong protest to the UN Security Council, protesting not only against his arrest and demanding his immediate release, but also elaborating on the essence of the functioning of The Hague Tribunal, and showing that this quasi-court is an exponent of the US administration. The fact that it has not yet reacted to the brutal violation of the UN charter and the open order for the bombing of a country and the killing of its people shows that `There is no need for an investigation and that this is not a court,'" he said. Then it has Mr. Sainovic presenting a document to journalists, and in the following paragraph: "All lower-rank bodies, various tribunals, SFORs and such-like, they are all in the service of NATO, and NATO, on its part, is nothing but a brutal executor of the US administration's policy." And then over the page, I suppose connected in the last paragraph: "If a country doesn't accept a US administration's ultimatum, NATO bombs it. If a television station shows programmes not to the administration's liking, NATO bombs it. If a politician says something opposed to US views, NATO arrests him." So those observations by the accused, through the mouth of his lawyer, as said to be, and under what other circumstances could Mr. Fila possibly have been speaking for him, tell against him, and we say in a way that is irrebuttable. The interview, we of course accept the clear jurisprudence to the effect that not to go for interview is no evidence of non-cooperation. Submitting oneself for interview, as again the Chamber indicated its finding, can be some indication of cooperation, and we would perhaps prefer to put it in this way: Can be a step on the way towards cooperation in certain circumstances. And so where people protest that they want to cooperate by interview, that position has to be tested. And this may be indeed what lay behind the particular observations of the Prosecutor on the last occasion, although of course we accept as definitive the Appeals Chamber's decision. But when someone does submit to questioning, if he says nothing of value and gives answers that are neither of value nor reflective of the reality, well, then, is that cooperation? Of course, an evaluation of an accused's interview is ultimately the matter for a Trial Chamber, and not for the Prosecution, but the Chamber may have absolutely no doubt that if a man in the position of Sainovic had cooperated by the method of interview, in a way that unravelled the questions facing the Prosecution and this court, there would have been every reason for the Prosecution to acknowledge that as a step of cooperation. We are quite unable to do so. His being interviewed remains on the jurisprudence a neutral fact. I think I've already dealt with the assertion about availability of documents from archives, but perhaps I should underline it in relation to some assertions about particular documents. If one of my learned friends was suggesting that there has been a complete unlocking of the minutes of the SDC in 1998 by provision of stenographic notes, I am not, I think, aware of that, and do not believe that there has been any general unlocking of the stenographic notes that exist and to which we have sought access for so long in an endeavour to assist the Trial Chamber in another case. So that's a further example of non-cooperation by the authorities and inappropriate reliance by those representing these accused. Mr. Fila suggested that they're always asked to give and that in some way the Prosecution would add to goodwill by not opposing provisional release. I must respectfully reject that approach. As I've already reminded the Chamber, we take an attitude, I think as probably Mrksic or Martic makes sure we should, individual by individual to applications of this kind and by no means do we always oppose them. We oppose them where we regard it as essential on the material available to us to do so, bearing in mind that even where we don't oppose applications for provisional release, the discretion is entirely a matter for the Chamber. Here, this accused was a fugitive for three years, in a state that protected him. There was absolutely no reason why he should not have got on a plane. There is absolutely no reason why, in the 18 months he was actually in office, he should not, as it appears he did not, prepare himself by access to documents he then had available to him for Defence. There is no reason why he shouldn't have communicated directly with the Prosecution about his intentions. None of those things did he do. I turn then to Ojdanic. The same observations about his surrender not being voluntary may be made. I turn to the statements that he made, which the Chamber will recall can be found in his application for provisional release annexed to it. And there were two pleadings on his behalf in relation to this application. It's perhaps important to observe that the statements which indeed the Prosecution rely on were annexed to the first of those pleadings, and we can see the first relevant document on page 12 of the numbered pages helpfully numbered at the bottom and in the middle, at least in the version I have. From Glas Javnosti of the 12th of February, 2002, an interview with the accused Ojdanic as follows: "The federal Ministry of Defence, during the 1999 war, Colonel General Ojdanic told the Glas newspaper that he would not surrender voluntarily. In an interview with a Glas journalist conducted in the Yugoslav army of installation in Dedinje, Ojdanic said he did not feel guilty because he had discharged his duty honourably. I am a soldier, and my duty was to defend the state and the people from aggression. All orders that I issued were in accordance with the Geneva Conventions and the rules of war. If I am guilty of anything, then our courts should decide." Now, I think in the first pleading, the second part of that statement was relied on, but there was no qualification as to the first part. We'll come to that a little later. The following page, page 13, again from April, but of the same year, 2002, under the heading "I will not surrender to The Hague Tribunal," this, Belgrade, April 3rd. "Former chief of the VJ General Staff, General Ojdanic, stated he would not turn himself into The Hague Tribunal. I am not afraid of the arrest, but I will turn myself in only if the Yugoslav parliament adopts the law on cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, emphasised General Ojdanic in a written statement submitted to the associated press by his family." We turn on two pages to page 17. This of interest, in the blocked passage in the middle of the page: "One of the accused, General Ojdanic, has protested in public, through his lawyer, because Serbian judiciary has not initiated criminal procedure against him based on The Hague Tribunal's indictment, even though he allegedly requested initialisation of the criminal procedure based on the indictment proclaimed in public, stating it's not -- he is not running away from his eventual responsibility but objects local organs their passivity." I'll come back to that when we look at the affidavit of this accused. And if you go over, however, one page to page 18, it has this passage recorded, for April 14th of 2002: "`At any moment, I expect to receive a court summons from the International Criminal Tribunal. With tranquility and dignity, I will respond to the summons and go to The Hague,' he was quoted as saying. `I waited for a word from the people, in other words, for a law on cooperation with the Tribunal to be adopted,' he said. `Departure to The Hague is now, I emphasise the word now, my legal obligation.'" The clearest and most flagrant denial of the supremacy of authority of this Tribunal which should, could, and one would have thought would have been available to him from an elementary consideration of Article 29 of our Statute and its associated Rule, to which I will refer you briefly by way of reminder in a moment. At page 25 of the same bundle, and at the foot of the page, under a headline of an associated press writer -- not a headline, a reference of an associated press writer of April 22nd, 2002: "Two key suspects of the UN war crimes court said Monday they would surrender to the Tribunal just hours before a Yugoslav government deadline expires for 23 people to turn themselves in or face arrest. General Ojdanic and former Croatian Serb leader Milan Martic submitted surrender papers to the Yugoslav justice ministry just before midday." Following paragraph: "A deadline surrender was extended from noon until midnight, after lawyers for several suspects contacted the ministry." Martic has, of course, as I reminded you, been refused provisional release. Thus then the statements that were relied upon, some or two of which to some extent the accused now seeks to challenge. But they were put forward unchallenged because he relied on them for other purposes in his first pleading. And it's only in the affidavit attached to the reply brief that we find any caviller with the terms of those documents, and we would invite the Chamber to say that those accounts given are clearly reliable and sustain absolutely the approach of the accused, which has been to enjoy the harbouring of his state as long as he could. This applies to both of them if they are returned on any terms to a country of entirely uncertain political future, who knows but that that harbouring would not recur. But in the affidavit which deals with and since the Chamber has read it, I won't take you through it in detail, in fact at all, the statement, which deals with those two observations by the accused, there's also the documents whereby it is said he sought to bring prosecution on himself locally, and those are documents that I'd invite you to reconsider, perhaps not now but at your leisure. They can be found on registry pages 7771 for the document to the chief military prosecutor of the 19th of November, 2001, and at registry page 7764 for the document dated the 20th of September. These are documents where, it is said, the accused was seeking trial on his home territory. It was and must be well known to the accused and a matter of really public knowledge that no senior person - and these are very senior people - has been brought to trial in their own territory. Second, if you look at the terms of the request, what the accused was really seeking to do, you may in our submission be quite satisfied was seeking to have some kind of public opportunity to put out the defence case in order that in a could be given a recognition that would defend him against prosecution. In his pleadings, this accused relies upon the advice he was given by lawyers, the same lawyers that represent him still. And so there is a parallel involvement of the lawyers, as in the case of Mr. Sainovic. I simply cannot understand how there can be the attempt to shelter behind such advice when Article 29 of the Statute, which of course any lawyer representing any accused or prospective accused before this Chamber would have reviewed, makes absolutely clear that states shall comply without undue delay with request for assistance in the surrender or the transfer of the accused to the Tribunal. And as the Tribunal well knows, the law of the Tribunal is superior to that of the local jurisdictions and indeed the relevant Rule, I think, we can find these matters further set out is Rule 58. So just to remind you of that. The obligations laid down in Article 29 of the Statute shall prevail over any legal impediment to the surrender or transfer of the accused or of a witness to the Tribunal which may exist under the national law or expedition treaties of the state concerned. So Your Honour, it's our position that it could hardly be clearer for either of these accused, but I focus for the moment on the accused Ojdanic. He took, so he says, legal advice. We don't know what question it was that was posed. To some degree, the privilege of lawyer/client seems to have penetrated, but I seek to take it no further. The answer he got was the answer that justified his staying where he was. That's all we really know. The remaining points on General Ojdanic, and I'm done really, are these: Mr. Robinson speaks of the Appeal Chamber dealing with the high status of Milutinovic. My reading of the decision is that the high status of the co-accused and of the accused generally is what is significant. High status they undoubtedly had. So far as guarantees are concerned, this: I think the authorities are clear that the primary issue is whether an accused will respond and will attend, and the Appeals Chamber decision on the material available which has not changed is clear. Personal guarantees really do not enter into the position, and guarantees of states, which are, for the reasons I've already explained, of only limited mid or long-term value, don't make the case different from what it is when you look at the individual as an individual. In any well-ordered society, there will be police who will bring to book those who are on provisional release or on bail. The fact that they may be successful in doing so in due course, if called upon to act, doesn't -- is not itself determinative of whether a person should be granted provisional release on bail. That decision is made by consideration of the factors that relate to him, so that the guarantees have limited value and in any event are of uncertain security in the circumstances that exist. Your Honour, I think that's all I want to say, but it's Mr. Shin who has helped us and the Chamber by the pleadings, in particular that you have before you. I'm going to check whether he or Ms. Romano have anything else they want to say. Probably he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Perhaps a couple of points for emphasis, and I'm grateful to Mr. Shin. So far as Milutinovic is concerned, the fact that Milutinovic has surrendered himself simply changes nothing. I think perhaps I made this point already. They've all been set out, our points on this, in our brief, in both cases. And what we've said in relation to Ojdanic applies equally to Sainovic. So far as the law is concerned, the Mrksic Appeals Chamber makes clear, and we summarise this in our pleadings, that the reliability of a guarantee given by the relevant authority has to be determined in relation to the circumstances of the particular case in which that guarantee arises. And if you're familiar with the Mrksic decision, it then goes on to deal with how a state's guarantee, in relation to two potentially different accused, could be relied upon differently, favourably to one but neutrally or negatively as to the other. That, I think, simply reinforcing the general point that I make, that A; they are accused specific in shorthand; and B, that they don't make good a case that cannot be made otherwise. It's up for the accused to satisfy the burden that falls on him as to the two elements he has to prove. And guarantees by state are very much a long stop that have only limited effect thereafter. Your Honour, I think that's probably all I have to add. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila, is there anything you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just to clarify certain things that are not correct or the result of a misunderstanding. It is clear that if this Tribunal is concerned with the individual criminal responsibility of an accused, that we cannot ask from him, the accused in this case, Sainovic, to bear the burden or to be the victim of a pace of cooperation. If we look at the guarantees, in light of that, the value of guarantees in case of Sainovic, that he would be brought here is that he is not enjoying any single privilege of this regime. Not at any point in time was he ordered to appear before the Tribunal upon the expiration of his mandate as a federal deputy, which expired on the 4th of February, I think. He arrived here at the time he arrived. Once again, I was not Defence counsel of Mr. Sainovic prior to the 24th of April. Not only do I not -- I don't remember such statements, but I claim here that I had never given any statement concerning Mr. Sainovic prior to the 24th of April, because I was not his Defence counsel at the time. I don't know about what journalists write, and it is true that I have been asked all kinds of questions by them. As far as the portion where Mr. Sainovic is mentioned is concerned, it was a press conference where he stated not his personal opinion but the opinion of the government and the party that he belonged to. He was acting as a spokesperson at that conference. It was not his opinion. He didn't demonstrate any personal disrespect of this Tribunal. I invite the Prosecutor to find such statement by Mr. Sainovic. If the requirement, if the condition for his temporary release is that I should stop defending him, then I would be prepared to withdraw. But let them bring the journalists. Let them state before the Tribunal that I had declared that as his Defence counsel. This can be easily seen from the record, from the files that can be found in this Tribunal. He was prosecuted together with Mr. Milutinovic, and one can clearly see that I was not his Defence counsel at the time. I would have defended him in Belgrade had I been his Defence counsel. This is simply not true that I was Defence counsel of Mr. Sainovic prior to the 24th of April. Therefore, whatever I stated is my problem, and I am prepared to be held responsible for that, but I did not give any such statement as a lawyer of Mr. Sainovic. As for the statements that are used by this Chamber, these are the statements that I state here before the Tribunal. I cannot be held accountable for things that are written by the media, such as some local Banja Luka paper. Once again, I was never -- I was not a Defence counsel of Mr. Sainovic prior to the 24th of April. Furthermore, I never said that I had access to the documents that the Prosecution does not have. Quite the contrary, there were many letters that were addressed to my country, to the effect that the documents -- that they were being provided some documents by the state. But I merely wish to be given the same opportunity. There is a law which regulates the access to the archives, and it is pursuant to that law that the Prosecutor has the right to inspect such archives, which right does not apply to me. I have never been given any such document. Formally speaking, this has been enabled in relevant legal provisions recently, but I have not seen them. And Mr. Sainovic cannot face consequences because of that. Mr. Nice is claiming that there are certain documents that exist, but on the other hand, the government of Serbia is claiming that such documents do not exist. I am referring to a number of documents in Pristina concerning a joint command that they allege existed at the time. Finally, to speak about the time limits. There is a decision of a supreme court of Serbia whereby some of the accused are not allowed to appear. That was the case with Milan Martic. If it is possible to kill a Prime Minister in a country such as Serbia, Mr. Djindjic, you can imagine what the situation is. There are no legal provisions to that respect as far as we are concerned. Sainovic spoke and he addressed the Assembly at the time when he wanted to tell them that he was willing to surrender. This was known to minister Batic and everybody else. They all knew that he would surrender as soon as the law on cooperation is adopted. He never relied upon immunity, he never requested anything, and that is why Mr. Nice has nothing specific to show that Mr. Sainovic stated anything personally on his behalf, nor did I state any such things as his Defence counsel. I don't remember about other statements. I wish to explain to the Chamber that it is a very good move -- it would be a very good move for this provisional release to be granted. The state of Serbia has taken upon itself to take him back whenever requested. The detention is not a punishment. I did not understand the Prosecutor. I'm not sure whether he meant to say that Serbia cannot be trusted, that the representative of Serbia and Montenegro clearly stated that they were willing to fulfil their obligations, which is what they did in the case of Milutinovic. So if we can be sure that Serbia will fulfil its obligations and Sainovic is willing to appear whenever summoned, I don't understand why we need this discussion at all. As soon as you tell him to come, he will appear, as was the case with Gruban, who was provisionally released, but he then came back and appeared for the Tribunal for a Status Conference and then he went back again. It would really be an act of goodwill of this Tribunal, if the number of 16 or 19 people who are still fugitives would be significantly decreased. And this is the kind of message in a should be sent by this Tribunal to the people who do not understand what else can be done. We have also inquired about the documents in question, but we were told that a lot of that burnt, that there had been a fire, and these are the documents referred to in the letter by Mr. Nice. He was talking about a witness that cannot be brought here. I assume it's Mr. Lilic. I'm not sure. But as far as I know, he never said that he was not willing to appear before the Tribunal. It is before this Chamber that he's supposed to testify. I can assure you that he will appear. As to whether he was relieved of his duty to confidentiality, I don't know, but I think that that can be easily dealt with. As for the stenographic notes, they were given and made available. Those were the stenographic notes of the minutes of the SPS. They were even given documents from the Supreme Defence Council. As to the value of those documents, I don't know. I really don't know whether Mr. Nice is telling the truth or not. I believe that he is. I don't know why he wouldn't. Perhaps this is not what he wanted, because this is not as valuable as he thought it would be, but this is all they have. If we sum up, I don't understand why Mr. Sainovic should be sitting here. Why? Because Serbia has failed to send some documents, a thing over which he has no competences at all? That is the crucial question. If the guarantees can be applicable for General Jokic and others and if Mr. Panceski is now telling you that people are reporting regularly that their whereabouts are known and controlled, I don't see where the problem is. These people will therefore appear whenever summoned. We discussed the issue with the Prosecutor. We never stopped discussing the issue. They did. They said: Well, let's wait for another month or a month and a half and then we will see how we will proceed. They said they were not satisfied with the interview. We lost nine days talking. Now, please do not tell me that they need nine days to see for themselves whether they like the result or not. I really don't understand. I really thought that the interview was very useful, but apparently that's not what they think. But the Chamber will have an opportunity to see for themselves, because this will constitute evidence before this Tribunal. And this is a demonstration of the respect that Mr. Sainovic has for in Tribunal, the fact that he has agreed to be interviewed. You can trust our word, Your Honour, and I can only give you my word once again that he will appear before the Tribunal when summoned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and I will be brief. First of all, I'd like to tell you the source of my information with respect to the Prosecutor's position on the release of President Milutinovic, and that is a newspaper article which appeared in Sunday in Serbia. Now, I fully accept Mr. Nice's representation that that's not the case, and I guess that's precisely our point, that relying on an article in a Serbian newspaper is no way to make a decision based on anything important, especially someone's freedom. I'm not going to spend a long time reading you newspaper articles, because I don't believe that that's the basis upon which you should decide this case, but I would just note that on page 29 of annex 1 to our provisional release application, when we attached all of the articles that were relevant, there was an article which quoted Florence Hartman, the spokeswoman for the Tribunal's chief prosecutor Carla Del Ponte, after General Ojdanic had surrendered and she was quoted as saying that she had nothing against the idea of Ojdanic awaiting his trial in Serbia. Now, we have provided the Court with a great deal of information upon which to base its decision, based on reliable evidence. Mr. Nice says that nothing in the pleadings changes the position regarding voluntary surrender from that which was before you in the first instance or before the Appeals Chamber and that's simply not correct, because what you had before you was simply a headline that said "I will not surrender" and what the Appeals Chamber had before it was that same article in which General Ojdanic was not even quoted as saying "I will not surrender" but which the headline was "I will not surrender." And so since then we've given you all of the articles which show that in fact his position was consistent. He preferred prosecution in his national system, he recognised the primacy of this Tribunal and he acted in accordance with that. And when the law in his country was adopted that said that notwithstanding the prohibition upon extradition of our citizens, we have them surrender to the Tribunal to be processed by the Tribunal, he did that. And so the articles in their totality show a man who in fact recognised his obligations and ultimately fulfilled them, and you said in your decision that it was the fact of surrender that was important. And I believe that was a very wise observation, and I think these newspaper articles notwithstanding, that remains true to this day. But we've also given you a very detailed affidavit from General Ojdanic which allows you to make your decision from facts not innuendo from newspaper articles and I hope you'll give that affidavit very serious consideration. Now, there's been a lot of discussion about documents and archives and lord knows as an American I'm about the last person who knows anything about the status of the cooperation between the Serbian Montenegro and this Tribunal with respect to documents, but I just harken you back to your own decision on provisional release in which you said that the suggestion was made that the government's level of cooperation was generally unsatisfactory. However, it is the particular level of cooperation relating to the issues of provisional release with which this application is concerned. In this connection, the Trial Chamber is satisfied that the proposed level of cooperation is satisfactory. That statement was not the subject of any criticism of the Appeals Chamber, and in fact Judge Hunt in his dissent noted that that was correct that it should not be general cooperation that burdens a particular accused but the level of cooperation with respect to provisional release. And that cooperation has been 100 per cent. Every person who has been given release based on a guarantee of the government of Serbian Montenegro and the Republic of Serbia has returned when requested and the government has been enforcing those guarantees. They report to the police station, they file their reports with this court. And so this court was correct in the first place and nothing changes that, either in circumstances or from what you've heard from Mr. Nice today. Now, there are several ways one can be a fugitive. You can go into hiding, you can vow not to be taken alive, but General Ojdanic wasn't doing that. He made efforts to see that he remained in Belgrade, that his whereabouts were known. He asked authorities to look into the possibility of prosecuting him. He was in contact with the ambassador from the United States even before his surrender. He took all of the steps of a person who has no intention of hiding or fleeing from their obligations. And when it became -- when the law was passed, he was the first to surrender, the first to publicly acknowledge that it was his duty to surrender, and he was an example for several other people who surrendered after him. And the bottom line is, you have to determine whether this particular man, General Ojdanic, can be trusted to come back when he's needed, and I think that his actions from the time that he learned of his indictment in 1999, through the time that he came to this Tribunal in 2002, show that this is a man who takes his obligations seriously, whose word is his bond, and who will, without doubt, be here every time he's needed, and that's really the issue before this Trial Chamber. Now, I just want to point out that despite all of the efforts that we've made to give you all the articles that contain public statements, to give you a detailed affidavit from General Ojdanic. On the other side of the ledger, the Prosecution has presented nothing, no evidence. They've offered no witness with declarations, they've offered no exhibits. They're simply trying to put their spin on newspaper articles, and they have nothing more. And I think that when you weigh the evidence, as I hope you will, the weight of the evidence is strongly in favour of General Ojdanic and in favour of your original conclusion that he will appear if released and that he will not be a danger to anyone. And I think that what has happened in the last ten months as he's waited in the Detention Unit has only shown how correct your original decision was. I want to just tell you about General Ojdanic's attitude towards this Tribunal, because I've known him, as indicated in his affidavit, now since May of 2001. And General Ojdanic respects the Tribunal, recognises its jurisdiction, and he is going to be here to fight his case, because he is an innocent man and he -- the time that he's spending in this Detention Unit is not something that's going to be credited to him when he's sentenced, because we expect that he's going to be acquitted by this Trial Chamber and that he won't be able to ever recover all of this time that he's lost. So, Your Honours, I would ask you to please consider the man General Ojdanic, consider his actions, and to grant our application for provisional release. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Panceski.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANCESKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do not wish to enter into a discussion or a polemic with any of the parties, but I would like to refer to a few points made here. I agree completely with Mr. Nice, who said that this should be decided on a case-by-case basis. Many objections relating to the alleged non-cooperation of Serbia and Montenegro with this Tribunal refer to the Milosevic case. Let me remind you that on the 10th of March, a hearing was held before this very Chamber, where the standpoints of the Prosecution and of Serbia and Montenegro were heard, and the Chamber decided that the government of Serbia and Montenegro should be given two months to respond to the motion by the Prosecution. My colleagues in Belgrade are currently considering this motion and, as representatives of a serious and responsible government, we shall comply with this deadline and submit our response within the required time period. But let me reiterate: This is a different case. We are now discussing the provisional release motion of Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Ojdanic. As regards the third accused in this case, the third accused in this indictment, the allegation by the Prosecution, and I quote: "Mr. Milutinovic was a fugitive who was protected by the state in his own interest." This absolutely does not correspond with the truth. After the change of government in October 2000, the new government clearly stated that they would comply with their international obligations and that Mr. Milutinovic would arrive in The Hague on the expiration of his term of office. He was then the president of the Republic of Serbia. Let me raise two more points in connection with the law on cooperation, because there is a particular provision that has been criticised, and this provision prohibits the handing over of persons accused after the law entered into force. I would like to say that there is a radical transformation under way in my country and that all legislation will be brought into line with the new political reality. On several occasions, officials of my country have pointed out that Article 39 will be changed. Let me address one more point; that is, the authorities in my country, it was said here, are unable to comply with their obligations. In cases such as that of Mrs. Plavsic or Momcilo Gruban, they did turn up for hearings in The Hague and then they went back to Belgrade, which shows that our government bodies are able and willing to meet their obligations. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. That concludes the hearing. We're grateful to the interpreters for going on rather longer. We'll consider these matters and give our decision in writing in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: adjourned at 4.14 p.m.
